issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: 'Comments on sexual violence' is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening accident in the absence of any sexual-trauma content elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals. This is not just unusual; it suggests a different trauma theme than the stated index event.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on how the event could have been prevented' can occur after accidents, but here the rest of the profile centers on sensory trauma cues and intrusive memory/avoidance rather than a coherent prevention-focused appraisal pattern. With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette: Seventy-two years old Miguel Hernandez, a respected cardiac surgeon at a busy New York hospital, recounts the night that turned his life into a series of flashes of a single moment. He was returning from a late-night elective procedure when a delivery truck skidded across the median of the highway. The impact was sudden, the sound a roar that reverberated through his chest. He survived with broken ribs and a fractured wrist, but the memory of that collision remains more vivid than any other life event. Miguel tells his therapist that the image of the crumpled bumper and the flash of bright headlights feels sharper than any surgical diagram he has ever studied. He admits that the memory often intrudes into his thoughts when he does not want it to, and that he finds himself pushing the scene away before he can fully recall it, even as the details flood his mind in an uncontrollable wave. The very sounds that once guided patients in the operating room now trigger Miguel to abandon his leisure. When the city's traffic hum or the distant clang of a car alarm echoes, he instinctively cancels a planned evening out with his wife. The texture of the seatbelt strap in his own car becomes a tactile trigger, a rough polymer that reminds him of the moment his body was ripped from its expected trajectory. In the hospital corridors, the sight of a colleague who was present at the accident, a face he recognizes, compels him to withdraw from conversations that would normally bring him joy. Each of these triggers forces Miguel to employ the maladaptive strategies he has adopted: giving up pleasant activities, steering clear of any situation that might physically stress him, and avoiding thoughts of the event itself. The chain reaction is swift; a single trigger leads straight to a retreat from the world he once navigated with confidence. Miguel's memories of the crash do more than haunt him; they shape the very strategies he has built to cope. The vividness of that night-he describes it as a living, breathing episode-makes the idea of confronting the event in his mind feel like stepping back into the wreck. Because the memory feels so immediate, he believes that thinking about it would be tantamount to reliving the pain. As a result, he consciously avoids any mental engagement with the accident, a strategy that allows him to feel safe in the present but also prevents him from processing the trauma. His decision to give up enjoyable activities, such as his weekly piano lessons and weekend hiking trips, stems directly from that memory's overwhelming presence. In the quiet moments before sleep, the unbidden images surge, and he resists the urge to let the mind wander, choosing instead to remain in the stillness of denial. The memory's hold on Miguel is not limited to his inner world; it reverberates outward, intensifying the triggers that surround him and deepening the cycle of avoidance. The more he distances himself from patients, colleagues, and even the familiar rhythm of the hospital, the more pronounced the sensory cues become. A surgical mask's texture or the clatter of instruments now echo the roughness of the seatbelt, and the sight of a loved one who once shared that fateful drive turns into a reminder of danger. His avoidance of the operating theater, once a hub of professional fulfillment, has turned into a trigger in itself: the knowledge that he cannot return to the OR amplifies his sense of loss and threat. By relinquishing his surgical duties, Miguel inadvertently magnifies the very stimuli that had once forced him to retreat, creating a loop in which each attempt to stay safe only brings him closer to the precipice he fears. After months of escalating dread and a steadily declining performance at work, Miguel finally sought therapy. He confided that the most frightening thought is the possibility of losing his surgical license, a dream that had guided his life for decades. Yet he also expressed a glimmer of hope, a desire to reclaim the control he once had over his body and his environment. He came to the clinic with the conviction that the only way forward is to untangle the web of memory, trigger, and avoidance that has bound him for years. The present moment feels like a crossroads: if he can learn to navigate the remnants of the crash without surrendering his life to fear, perhaps he can heal enough to return to the operating room-and to the life he has long shared with his wife.
